messages.author: da6d9613ff0dac62
messages.subject: error in growth models with multiple imputed data
parts:
I am using Multiple imputation data to fit parallel models. I have checked variable models individually to ensure best fit but when I combine some of the variables into a parallel model I get this error (
Error in D3.LRT(object, h1 = h1, useImps = useImps, asymptotic = asymptotic, : D3 test statistic could not be calculated. Try the D2 pooling method.), which I am not sure what it means, or how to fix it.

Another few questions:
1- After plotting some of my variables I see that there is a positive trend and then a decline afterward, as well as extremely large variability in response within same participant. Would this lead to negative variances in time points and/or slope & intercept variance? Do I need to worry about that? Would this be considered a Heywood case as well?

2- This might be a silly question but I don't quite understand why to models that are perfectly fitted when analyzed individually lead to a bad fit when combined into a parallel model. What should I do in this case? Some of my data is extremely variable as a group as well as within the same participant, how do you deal with this issue? I've tried every different possibility  in order to get the best fit (i.e. quadratics, picewise, etc.)

3- Is also not uncommon  that when running parallel growth models with multiple imputed data I might get:
Negative test statistic set to zero 

Negative pooled test statistic was set to zero, so fit will appear to be arbitrarily perfect. 

Why is that? How do I fix this? Should I worry about overfitting if my RMSEA=0, CFI=1 etc?


Any help on this would be much appreciated!

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: error in growth models with multiple imputed data
parts:
I get this error (
Error in D3.LRT(object, h1 = h1, useImps = useImps, asymptotic = asymptotic, : D3 test statistic could not be calculated. Try the D2 pooling method.), 
which I am not sure what it means, or how to fix it.
It means the default D3 test statistic could not be calculated (not sure why), and you can fix it by setting test="D2" when you call lavTestLRT.mi() or anova() (see the ?lavTestLRT.mi help page).
Do I need to worry about that? Would this be considered a Heywood case as well?

Any negative variance is a Heywood case.  If your model fits poorly, that could be an explanation.  If not, sampling error is another (in my experience, much more commonly) plausible explanation.  You can test the H0 that the variance is truly nonnegative by inspecting whether the 95% CIs include positive values, in which case it is consistent with sampling variability.

https://doi.org/10.1177%2F0049124112442138
I don't quite understand why to models that are perfectly fitted when analyzed individually
lead to a bad fit when combined into a parallel model
Not sure what this means.  Are you referring to a pooled chi-squared, or are you comparing different modeling approaches?

Negative pooled test statistic was set to zero, so fit will appear to be arbitrarily perfect. 

Why is that?

That can happen due to sampling error, especially when the model fits well.  The D3 statistic involves complicated calculations, including fitting the model with parameter estimates fixed at pooled values to each imputation.  If I recall correctly, the D3 pooled stat can be negative when the fixed-model fit is better on average across imputations than the average LRT stat across imputations... something like that. 

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
